Kümmel.et: From Middle High German kümel, kumel, from Old High German kumil, from Proto-West Germanic *kumil (“caraway, cumin (seed)”).

Kümmelblättchen.et: From Kümmel (“caraway”) + Blättchen (“little card”). The first element is actually a folk etymology, and is an alteration of Hebrew גִּימֶל (gímel, “the third letter of the Hebrew alphabet”).

kümmern.et:
From Middle High German kumbern, derived from the noun kumber, probably from Old French *combre (“obstruction, barrier”), itself probably from Gaulish. See Kummer for more.
Cognate with Hunsrik kimmre, Luxembourgish këmmeren and Dutch kommer.

Kummerbund.et:
Borrowed from English cummerbund, from Hindustani کمر بند / कमरबंद (kamarband), from Classical Persian کمربند (kamarband), derived from کمر (kamar, “waist”) + بند (band, “band”).

Kumpf.et: From Middle High German kumpf, kumph (also kump, komp), from Old High German *kumpf, *kump, *kumb, from Proto-Germanic *kumbaz.

s: friend in the same business (male or of unspecified gender)
Kumpan.et: From Middle High German kompān, kumpān, from Old French compain (“friend; companion”), from Late Latin compāniō (literally “he with whom one shares one's bread”), from com- + pānis (with + bread).

Kummet.et: From Middle High German komat, kommet, borrowed from Upper Sorbian chomot, from Proto-Slavic *xomǫtъ. Compare Polish chomąto.

Kumys.et: Borrowed from Russian кумыс (kumys), from Turkic.

s: a receptacle for depositing any kind of emotional burden, usually in written form (sorrow, worries, anger, discontent, etc.)

Kumpe.et: From Kumpan + -e, with retraction of the accent to the first syllable.
